title: Job 40:6–14
context: The LORD answers Job again out of the whirlwind, beginning his second speech with the same summons as the first (compare Job 38:3). He asks whether Job will annul his judgment and condemn him so that Job may be justified, and whether Job has an arm like God and a voice that thunders. He then invites Job to clothe himself with majesty, pour out his anger on the proud, humble them, and crush the wicked, and says that if Job can do this, the LORD will admit that Job’s own right hand can save him. The key line, 40:8, rebukes Job for defending his own righteousness at the expense of God’s justice (compare Job 19:6; 27:6; 32:2), without endorsing the friends’ claim that Job’s suffering proves his guilt; the book later says the friends have not spoken what is right as Job has (Job 42:7). Arminian and Reformed readers generally agree that God is just, that Job was not being punished for hidden sin, and that a creature should not vindicate himself by condemning God. Arminian readers commonly stress that God’s justice is real goodness that Job will come to trust, though he cannot yet see it; Reformed readers commonly stress the Creator’s rightful sovereignty, which the creature is not placed to judge (compare Romans 9:20; Isaiah 45:9). Both emphases are commonly held together, and neither tradition reads the verse as calling Job wicked.

verses.text: Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind:
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD answering Job again out of the whirlwind. Job’s silence is not the end of the conversation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD continuing to address Job in majesty (compare Job 38:1). Readers in both traditions commonly read the second speech as further grace toward Job.

verses.text: “Now brace yourself like a man. I will question you, and you will answer me.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD calling Job to brace himself like a man and answer his questions. Job is treated as a real conversation partner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD repeating the summons of Job 38:3. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the LORD taking Job seriously while correcting him.

verses.text: Will you even annul my judgment? Will you condemn me, that you may be justified?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD rebuking Job for condemning him so that Job may be justified. They commonly stress that God’s justice is truly good even when unseen, without the friends’ charge of guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD rebuking self-justification at God’s expense, stressing the Creator’s rightful sovereignty (compare Romans 9:20). Both traditions commonly agree that God is just and that the verse does not call Job wicked (compare Job 42:7).

verses.text: Or do you have an arm like God? Can you thunder with a voice like him?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Job has an arm like God or a voice that thunders. Job lacks the power to judge the world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast between Creator and creature made plain. Readers in both traditions commonly read the question as showing why Job cannot sit in judgment on God.

verses.text: “Now deck yourself with excellency and dignity. Array yourself with honor and majesty.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD inviting Job to clothe himself with majesty and honor. The invitation exposes the gap between Job and God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the ironic challenge as highlighting God’s unique glory. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to humility, not mockery of Job’s suffering.

verses.text: Pour out the fury of your anger. Look at everyone who is proud, and bring him low.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD inviting Job to pour out his anger and bring down the proud. Judging the world justly requires more than human power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God alone as able to humble the proud (compare Isaiah 2:11; Luke 1:51–52). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as pointing to God’s rule over evil.

verses.text: Look at everyone who is proud, and humble him. Crush the wicked in their place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD challenging Job to humble every proud person and crush the wicked. Only God can govern justice on that scale.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereign authority over the wicked. Both traditions commonly read the verse as answering Job’s complaint about the prosperity of the wicked with a call to trust God’s rule.

verses.text: Hide them in the dust together. Bind their faces in the hidden place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD challenging Job to hide the wicked in the dust and bind their faces in the hidden place. Final justice belongs to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the imagery of judgment that God alone can carry out. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s challenge, not a literal instruction.

verses.text: Then I will also admit to you that your own right hand can save you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that if Job could do these things, he would admit Job’s own right hand could save him. Salvation is beyond human power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see salvation as belonging to God alone (compare Psalm 98:1; Isaiah 59:16). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about human dependence on God.
